framing: Why a fast model can still feel slow
paragraphs: When someone calls a model slow, they might mean one of two things: the answer took too long to begin, or it arrived in a stutter. Those complaints come from different work on different parts of the GPU, so a fix for one can do nothing for the other, or make it worse.

Serving runs in two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one burst of parallel arithmetic. Decode then produces one token at a time, and for each token it streams the model's weights out of memory. That's why the same chip can hit a compute limit in one phase and a memory limit in the next.

We'll take one short trace and read it closely, from the send to the last token. Then we'll put numbers on the two ceilings and on the cache that grows with every token, using arithmetic you can check by hand.

This is the vocabulary for everything that follows. Paging, prefix reuse, scheduling, and quantization each answer a limit you'll meet here, so get the clocks and the bytes straight before you touch a setting.
outcomes: Work out time to first token, time per output token, and both tokens-per-second rates from a trace.
Explain why prefill tends to hit a compute ceiling and single-stream decode a memory ceiling.
Estimate how much cache a workload needs before you buy or book the hardware.
question: Users say the assistant feels slow, yet the GPUs look busy and errors are flat. What would you measure first, and what would each answer tell you to change?
